segments.title: The Fog and the System: Opening into Chancery

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at one of the greatest novels in the English language.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through Bleak House chapter by chapter — its fog and its fury, its comedy and its grief.
Joining me today are three readers who bring very different but beautifully complementary lenses to this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is obsessed — in the best possible sense — with how Dickens builds his effects sentence by sentence.
She sees the architecture where the rest of us just see the building.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows the real institutions behind Dickens's world — Chancery, the poor law, the class machinery — from the inside out.
When James speaks about what poverty actually meant in Victorian England, you feel the weight of it.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read Bleak House as a teenager and has returned to it more times than she can count.
She is our guide to the experience of reading — what stops you cold, what makes you laugh, what you carry with you long after you close the book.
Today we are entering the world Dickens builds in Bleak House — a world thick with fog, tangled in law, and haunted by the question of identity.
James, I'd like to begin with you — because the passages you've been looking at go to the very heart of what this novel is about: the way the system grinds people into invisibility.
Thank you — and yes, that word 'invisibility' is exactly right.
One of the passages I've been sitting with is from early in the novel — the death of Nemo, the law-writer who lodges above Krook's shop.
He is a man of forty-five years, and when he dies there is nothing — no record, no connection, no traceable thread back into the world.
Dickens gives us this image, and it is one of the most devastating in the book.
The lonely figure on the bed lies there with — and I'm quoting directly — 'no more track behind him that any one can trace than a deserted infant.'
A deserted infant — that is the image Dickens reaches for.
Not a broken old man, not a failed adult — an abandoned child, with nothing before and nothing behind.
That compression of a whole life into a single simile is, to my mind, one of the great moral indictments in Victorian fiction.
James, that image works because it collapses time as well as identity.
Five and forty years — that phrase is placed with such deliberateness right before the simile.
Dickens tells you the quantity of life first — the span of it — and then immediately cancels all that duration with a single image of nothingness.
The coffin standing ready by the old portmanteau — that detail is doing extraordinary work too.
The portmanteau is a traveling object — it implies journeys, a life in motion — and it stands next to a box that goes nowhere.
That's visual poetry, and it's structural — the whole novel is built on that kind of quiet juxtaposition.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is the phrase 'all that night.'
The coffin stands there through an entire night — time passing, indifferent, while this man simply ceases.
There's no witness, no mourner, no one to mark the hours.
And it makes you think forward in the novel to the secrets that cling to Nemo — to Lady Dedlock, to Esther — all of it already present in this quiet, terrible room.
And that secrecy is never just personal in this novel — it is always enforced by something structural.
The passage about Lady Dedlock's sister — the woman who became Esther's mother — is one of the most chilling demonstrations of that.
Jarndyce is recounting how she cut herself off from Boythorn — the man who loved her — not out of spite, but out of a terrible, internalised code of honour.
The language Dickens gives Jarndyce is almost unbearable in its precision.
'She wrote him that from the date of that letter she died to him — as in literal truth she did.'
'And that the resolution was exacted from her by her knowledge of his proud temper and his strained sense of honour, which were both her nature too.'
'She made the sacrifice, she said, and would live in it and die in it.'
Live in it and die in it — that is a kind of slow self-annihilation carried out with perfect composure.
And what makes it historically resonant is that this was not an unusual fate — the class and honour system produced exactly these choices for women, generation after generation.
'Both her nature too' — that parenthetical is the thing that haunts me.
She destroys herself using the very instrument that was used to shape her — the pride, the honour, the rigid self-control.
Dickens is saying something very precise about how ideology internalises — how the cage becomes the self.
And structurally, this passage is placed so that we understand Lady Dedlock before we judge her — Dickens is always doing that, putting the cause before the verdict.
And then you arrive at Mrs. Rouncewell's plea to Lady Dedlock, and suddenly that architecture of pride and silence has a human cost standing right in front of it.
This is one of the most moving scenes in the book for me.
Mrs. Rouncewell has served this family her whole life, and she comes to Lady Dedlock not with accusation but with pure, anguished appeal.
The passage that gets me every single time is this one.
'My Lady, you may have some proud or angry reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know;'
'if so, pray, oh, pray, think of a faithful servant whose whole life has been passed in this family which she dearly loves.'
'Pray, oh, pray' — the repetition is not rhetoric, it is someone actually begging.
And the way she names Lady Dedlock's distance — 'one far away from themselves who can't be approached close' — she is describing a whole social order, not just one woman.
And Dickens is scrupulous to tell us that her simplicity is genuine — 'the old housekeeper pleads with genuine simplicity.'
That is important, because in another kind of novel Mrs. Rouncewell might be a comic figure — the loyal retainer with her station and her dignity.
Here she is a woman whose class position is in direct tension with her need — she must ask for help from the very hierarchy that defines her as lesser.
That is not sentiment — that is a precise diagnosis of how class works, and it has not dated.

What strikes me listening to all of this is how consistently Dickens places the cost of secrecy and pride on the most vulnerable — on Nemo with his unmarked life, on Esther's mother, on Mrs. Rouncewell's son.
The fog at the opening of Bleak House is not just weather — it is the atmosphere of a system designed to obscure and erase.
We'll be returning to these threads throughout the series.
Coming up, we'll be turning to the novel's great comic machinery and asking how Dickens uses laughter to say the things that grief alone cannot.

segments.title: The Weight of Narrative Layers: How Dickens Builds Unreliability

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great labyrinthine novel seriously — one passage, one argument, one revelation at a time.
I'm your host, and today we're going deep into something that sits at the very heart of what makes this novel so uncanny: the weight of its narrative layers.

Dickens gives us two narrators — Esther Summerson's intimate first person, and an omniscient voice of extraordinary pressure and range — and he plays them against each other with a kind of structural genius.
Joining me to unpick how that works are three people who have thought about this novel more carefully than almost anyone I know.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who specialises in the architecture of fiction — how effects are built, sentence by sentence, image by image.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who can tell us what Chancery actually was and why it mattered — and why it should still make us angry.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and reads it with the attention of someone who never takes a single sentence for granted.

Eleanor, I want to start with you, because the passages we're looking at today cover an extraordinary range — a dead man lying in a tenement, Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn circling each other, and Snagsby descending into Tom-all-Alone's.
What is the omniscient narrator doing in these passages that Esther simply could not do?
The omniscient narrator in Bleak House is one of the strangest and most powerful voices in all of Victorian fiction.
It's not a godlike presence handing down comfortable truths — it's a voice under pressure, a voice that sees too much and sometimes seems barely able to contain what it knows.
Look at what happens in the chapter after Nemo dies.
The narrator suddenly breaks from observation into something almost like a lament — a direct, anguished address.
The line that stops me every time is this:
"where is she, while these ashes are above the ground!"
That is not narration — that is grief wearing the costume of narration.
Esther could never write that sentence — she didn't know this man, she didn't know the woman who might have loved him.
What strikes me about that passage is the way Dickens moves through time in a single paragraph.
He takes us back to infancy — the child at the mother's breast — and then forward to a lost love, and then back to the present corpse.
And all of that movement is framed by the silence after the Harmonic Meeting — the jingling piano finally gone quiet.
The irony of that social noise giving way to this absolute solitude — it's devastating.
And what Dickens is doing technically — what Eleanor is pointing at — is using the omniscient narrator to perform the mourning that no character in the novel can perform.
No one claims Nemo.
So the narrative voice becomes the only mourner he gets.
That's exactly right, and it has a precise social meaning that I don't think we should pass over too quickly.
A man like Nemo — a law-writer, paid by the page, living in a rented room above a rag-and-bottle shop — would in reality leave almost no institutional trace.
No will, no pension, no parish record that anyone would bother to retrieve.
The omniscient narrator is, in a very specific sense, compensating for the complete failure of every social institution to account for this man's existence.
And Dickens knew that system from the inside — he had watched men disappear into exactly this kind of anonymity.
James, that reading makes the structural choice even more resonant — because the omniscient narrator doesn't just mourn Nemo, it also watches, and accuses.
And nowhere is that double function — witness and prosecutor — more concentrated than in the Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn passages.
Dickens gives us their social surface — the exhausted deity, the speechless repository — and then refuses to let us rest there.
The passage is extraordinary — listen to what he does:

"But whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares; what each would give to know how much the other knows — all this is hidden, for the time, in their own hearts."
He tells us that information is being withheld — and then withholds it.
The omniscient narrator is performing its own version of the secret it's describing.
That's a remarkable observation — the narrator as a kind of double agent.
Caroline, you've re-read this novel more times than you can count — does that passage ever stop being unsettling?
Never.
And I think it's because Dickens has built Lady Dedlock and Tulkinghorn as two systems of concealment facing each other — and neither one blinks.
"Lady Dedlock is always the same exhausted deity, surrounded by worshippers, and terribly liable to be bored to death, even while presiding at her own shrine."
That phrase — 'her own shrine' — is doing so much work.
She is the object of worship and the prisoner of it at the same time.
And Tulkinghorn's description — 'the speechless repository of noble confidences' — is equally magnificent.
He doesn't speak; he accumulates.
And the narrator, watching them both, is doing exactly the same thing — accumulating what it will not yet release.
The power dynamic in those scenes has a very particular legal flavour that I find myself thinking about whenever I re-read them.
Tulkinghorn is a solicitor — a man whose entire professional value rests on holding other people's secrets safely.
But what Dickens shows us is that the custody of a secret is itself a form of power — and Tulkinghorn has understood this with terrifying clarity.
There's a line in the later confrontation that makes my blood run cold every time:
"Lady Dedlock, have the goodness to stop and hear me, or before you reach the staircase I shall ring the alarm-bell and rouse the house."
The calm of that.
He doesn't raise his voice — the narrator is explicit about that — and yet what he is threatening is total social annihilation.
That is a portrait of institutional cruelty dressed in perfect manners.
And he doubles down on that in the very next chapter — Tulkinghorn tells Lady Dedlock something extraordinary about the scale of his achievement in gaining this power over her.
He says — and I find this one of the most gothic lines in the novel —
"I would as soon have hoped to root up by means of my own strength and my own hands the oldest tree on this estate as to shake your hold upon Sir Leicester."
The metaphor is a tree — something natural, deep-rooted, almost sacred — but he has found a way to uproot it anyway.
What's chilling is that he almost admires what he's about to destroy.
That combination — admiration and annihilation — is where the gothic horror of Tulkinghorn lives.
The social and the gothic — they keep folding into each other in this novel.
James, you mentioned institutional cruelty — and I want to bring in the Tom-all-Alone's passage, because Snagsby's descent into that street is one of the most viscerally gothic moments in the novel.
What is the omniscient narrator doing there that is different from what it does in the Dedlock drawing room?
The Dedlock scenes are about concealment — the narrator withholds what it knows about hidden interiors.
Tom-all-Alone's is the opposite — Dickens insists on exposure, on making you look at what respectable London has refused to see.
The description of the street itself is almost a public health indictment:

"a villainous street, undrained, unventilated, deep in black mud and corrupt water — though the roads are dry elsewhere — and reeking with such smells and sights that he, who has lived in London all his life, can scarce believe his senses."
That parenthetical — 'though the roads are dry elsewhere' — is the political knife in the sentence.
It tells you that this filth is not natural disaster — it is manufactured inequality.
Dickens knew exactly what the sanitary reformers of the 1840s and 50s were arguing, and he turned their language into art.
And Snagsby is such a perfect vehicle for that scene — because he is respectable, and deeply anxious, and utterly out of his depth.
He has lived in London all his life — the narrator says so — and he cannot believe what he is seeing.
That's Dickens making a point about the geography of ignorance — how the city keeps its suffering invisible to those with the luxury of not looking.
And the image of going 'deeper down into the infernal gulf' — it's borrowed from Dante, almost, but made completely local and physical.
The omniscient narrator is letting us feel Snagsby's subjective terror while simultaneously refusing to let us retreat from the objective reality causing it.
That dual focus — inside and outside simultaneously — is exactly what the omniscient narrator can do that Esther cannot, and it matters enormously for the novel's design.
Esther's narration is warm, generous, occasionally unreliable in ways she can't quite see — she understates her own suffering, she misreads her own importance.
But there's a moment where Esther's unreliability is almost heartbreaking — Richard's confession to her.
He says to her, in his frankest manner:
"I understand you, and I wish to heaven I were a more constant sort of fellow... constant to myself."
He knows his own flaw — he names it with painful precision.
And yet Esther records it without the novel allowing us to feel the full catastrophe it foreshadows — because she loves him, and love limits what she'll let herself see.
That's where the two narrative voices become genuinely unreliable in opposite directions — one sees too much and withholds it; the other sees through love and cannot fully grasp what she hears.
Two kinds of unreliability, built into the architecture itself — one structural, one emotional.
We'll carry that tension forward — in a moment, we'll look at how Dickens uses these narrative layers to make the novel's central mystery almost unbearably slow to resolve.
Stay with us.
Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's great sprawling masterwork and examines it one passage at a time.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the novel's most quietly devastating threads: the slow unravelling of Richard Carstone.
We're in Chapter Thirteen — and already, beneath all the tenderness and young love, the shadows are gathering.
Joining me today are three brilliant readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose passion is the architecture of fiction — how the smallest structural choices carry the greatest weight.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who brings the real institutional world behind Dickens's pages — and isn't shy about his feelings on Victorian injustice.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens, and who brings an extraordinary ear for its verbal music.
Let's begin with the scene where Richard and Ada tell Esther they're in love — and the response that Esther, and then Mr. Jarndyce, give them.
What strikes me first about this scene is how Esther positions herself within it.
Richard and Ada put her between them — physically, literally — and she becomes the fulcrum of this young love.
And then she offers this wonderful admission — that she let them run on in their happiness because she was enjoying it too much herself.
She says, and this is the passage I keep coming back to:
"They went on in their own wild way for a little while — I never stopped them; I enjoyed it too much myself."
That parenthetical confession is pure Esther — self-deprecating but utterly human.
She is the moral centre of this novel, and yet here she admits to simply delighting in two young people being foolishly in love.
It makes you trust her completely.
Yes — and notice what Dickens does with the structure of that scene once the delight settles.
Esther guides them from rapture toward something harder: the language of duty.
She says this love could come to happiness only — and that word 'only' is doing enormous work —
"if it were real and lasting and inspired them with a steady resolution to do their duty to each other, with constancy, fortitude, and perseverance, each always for the other's sake."
Three abstract nouns stacked up like that — constancy, fortitude, perseverance — it's almost a legal formula.
And the irony — because Dickens is always working in irony — is that Richard will fail on every single one of those counts.
The virtues Esther names here become the precise map of Richard's destruction.
I want to come at this from a slightly different angle — because what Jarndyce does when he speaks to Richard matters enormously in its social context.
Jarndyce is not Richard's father, not his guardian in any formal sense — he says so himself, quite deliberately.
He says: "I am only your friend and distant kinsman. I have no power over you whatever."
That disclaimer is not modesty — it is a precise legal and social statement about the limits of his authority.
In a world where patriarchal control of young men's careers was near-absolute, Jarndyce is explicitly refusing to exercise it.
Which makes Richard's subsequent failures all the more his own.
No one can be blamed but Richard — and Dickens sets that up very carefully here.
And that's before Jarndyce even gets to the really extraordinary speech about Providence and effort.
There's something almost Old Testament about the rhetoric of it — and then suddenly Dickens drops in this comic detail about a heathen waggoner.
The full passage reads:
"Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never separate the two, like the heathen waggoner."
It's such an odd, vivid image — and it lands with the weight of an actual maxim.
Jarndyce is brilliant here — moral and funny in the same breath.
What I find structurally remarkable about that whole speech is how Jarndyce keeps layering the conditions.
It builds and builds until it arrives at this ultimatum that's almost breathtaking in its bluntness:

"If you entertain the supposition that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts, leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here."
The repetition — 'ever was or could be, ever will or can be' — that's oratorical rhythm used as a kind of moral hammer.
And he ends by putting Ada on the same level as the bad idea Richard must abandon.
Leave the wrong idea — or leave Ada.
It's devastating — and Richard, of course, will eventually leave both.
This is where the novel becomes genuinely tragic rather than merely satirical — and the medical subplot in Chapter Seventeen sharpens that contrast brilliantly.
Mrs. Badger's assessment of Richard is delivered with such polite precision that it almost hides how damning it is.
She says Richard feels the profession is simply — and I love this word — 'tiresome.'
And then she sets up the comparison with Woodcourt — the man who will eventually tend to Richard's broken body — with this:

"Young men like Mr. Allan Woodcourt who take it from a strong interest in all that it can do will find some reward in it through a great deal of work for a very little money and through years of considerable endurance and disappointment."
The irony is architectural — Woodcourt's vocation is defined precisely in the terms Richard can never embody.
Endurance. Disappointment. Years of it.
Richard cannot sustain anything long enough to discover whether it was worth sustaining.
And then Dickens gives us that image at the end of Chapter Thirteen — and it is one of the most beautiful and heartbreaking passages in the entire novel.
Richard and Ada walk away through the sunlit rooms, and Esther watches them go.
I'll read it — because this really has to be heard:

"So young, so beautiful, so full of hope and promise, they went on lightly through the sunlight as their own happy thoughts might then be traversing the years to come and making them all years of brightness."
"So they passed away into the shadow and were gone. It was only a burst of light that had been so radiant. The room darkened as they went out, and the sun was clouded over."
That final sentence — six words — 'the sun was clouded over.'
It's a weather report and a prophecy simultaneously.
Dickens never overloads it with explanation — he trusts the image completely.
The triple anaphora — 'So young, so beautiful, so full of hope' — sets up a rhythm of expectation.
And then the pivot: 'so they passed away into the shadow.'
The same syntactic shape — 'so' — but now it carries death and loss.
Dickens smuggles the catastrophe inside the same sentence architecture as the celebration.
That is what I mean by architecture carrying meaning — you feel the fall before you understand it.
What's remarkable is that all of this — the tenderness, the warning, the shadow — happens before Richard has made a single catastrophic choice.
Dickens loads the gun in Chapter Thirteen, and then we spend the rest of the novel watching it fire.
Thank you all — Eleanor, James, Caroline — for that close and careful reading.
Next, we turn to the institution that shadows all of Richard's choices — Chancery itself — and what it does to the people trapped inside it.

segments.title: Secrets and Shame: Lady Dedlock's Impossible Position

utterances.text: Welcome back to Bleak House Unpacked.
We're deep in the novel now, and the currents running beneath its surface are growing more dangerous by the chapter.
Today we're focusing on secrets, shame, and the way Chancery reaches into private lives and quietly ruins them.
Lady Dedlock stands at the centre of all that, but she's not the only one being unmade by forces she cannot control.
Eleanor Hartley is here as our literary critic, always alive to how Dickens builds his effects at the level of sentence and scene.
James Blackstone brings the legal and institutional history — he knows exactly what kind of machinery is grinding away behind Tulkinghorn's polished manners.
And Caroline Woodcourt reads as a devoted lifelong reader — she cares about what these moments feel like from the inside.
Let's begin with the moment Tulkinghorn's message arrives — that quietly devastating postscript Sir Leicester reads aloud to his wife.
What strikes me first about that scene is the machinery Dickens uses to deliver the blow.
Sir Leicester fumbles with his eyeglass, loses his place in the letter, searches for the right passage — all of that delay is doing real structural work.
We're told, quite pointedly, that Lady Dedlock looks a little irritated.
And when Sir Leicester finally lands on the postscript, he reads it aloud in full — and what we hear is Tulkinghorn's voice, dressed in formal courtesy.
He says, quite literally,
'I have something to tell her on her return in reference to the person who copied the affidavit in the Chancery suit, which so powerfully stimulated her curiosity. I have seen him.'
That final three-word sentence — 'I have seen him' — lands like a door closing.
Tulkinghorn knows exactly what he's doing, and so does Dickens.
That message is a legal document in miniature, delivered socially.
Tulkinghorn frames it as a courtesy — compliments to my Lady, hoping she has benefited by the change of air.
But every Victorian reader would have recognised the form: the lawyer communicating to his client that he holds information which may be consequential.
It is a warning wrapped in a pleasantry — and Sir Leicester reads it entirely straight, completely blind to its menace.
His fumbling with the eyeglass, which Eleanor rightly identifies as structural, is also socially revealing.
Sir Leicester lives at such a remove from urgency that he cannot even imagine his wife might be counting the seconds.
That gap between his obliviousness and her concealed terror is where the novel places almost unbearable dramatic irony.
Reading it — actually reading it on the page — I find Lady Dedlock almost unbearable to watch in that moment.
She looks a little irritated, the narrator tells us — and that is all.
The extraordinary discipline of that — to render someone in terror as merely appearing slightly impatient.
And then I think of Jo, in an entirely different register, with no armour whatsoever.
He cannot hide anything.
He wipes his eyes with his wretched sleeve and says,
'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'
The novel holds these two worlds — Lady Dedlock's frozen composure and Jo's open grief — and asks us to feel the distance between them.
That contrast is one of Dickens's great structural gifts — holding opposite registers in tension simultaneously.
Jo's grief for Nemo is entirely public, entirely unguarded, and it's expressed in a dialect that signals to every reader exactly how little social protection he has.
Lady Dedlock, by contrast, cannot afford a single unguarded syllable.
And what connects them — what the novel quietly insists on — is that Nemo is the thread running through both their stories.
He was kind to Jo.
He was the secret Lady Dedlock cannot outrun.
And it's worth staying with what Nemo actually represents in systemic terms.
He is someone the law has rendered literally nameless — a law-writer who copied documents for a system that destroyed him.
Jo weeps for him with a fullness of feeling the Court of Chancery would never register or record.
Which brings us, inevitably, to Richard Carstone — because Chancery doesn't only destroy the anonymous poor.
It destroys the hopeful young as well, in a different register but with equal thoroughness.
Richard Carstone — let's go there.
Caroline, you've read and re-read the passage where Richard tries to explain himself to Esther, and you've called it one of the saddest monologues in the novel.
It is.
Because Richard knows.
He knows what's being done to him, and he has the eloquence to describe it precisely, and it makes no difference at all.
He builds this whole extended metaphor — the unfinished house — and it's devastating because it's so accurate.
Let me read it, because the rhythm of it matters.

'If you lived in an unfinished house, you couldn't settle down in it; if you were condemned to leave everything you undertook unfinished, you would find it hard to apply yourself to anything; and yet that's my unhappy case.'

'I was born into this unfinished contention with all its chances and changes, and it has gone on unsettling me ever since; and here I am now, conscious sometimes that I am but a worthless fellow to love my confiding cousin Ada.'
'A worthless fellow to love my confiding cousin Ada' — that self-knowledge doesn't save him.
It just makes the watching more painful.
The conditional clauses doing that work — 'if you lived,' 'if you were condemned' — Dickens is constructing a logical proof from Richard's own mouth.
Richard is essentially demonstrating that his paralysis is rational, given his circumstances.
He cannot be argued out of it, because the argument is the problem.
Chancery has given him a completely coherent worldview in which nothing he does can matter until the suit is settled.
It's a closed loop — and the novel understands it as a kind of possession.
This is historically precise, and I think it's worth saying so.
Chancery suits in the first half of the nineteenth century could run for generations.
Entire families organised their futures around an expected inheritance that existed only as a legal possibility, perpetually deferred.
So Richard's unsettlement is not a personal failing dressed up in metaphor — it is a documented social pathology.
Dickens is reporting something, not inventing it.
The difference is that he gives it to us through a young man in love, which is the thing that makes it hurt.
And Ada sees it all, and loves him anyway, and looks forward in the most heartbreaking way.
There's a passage — Esther records it — where Ada imagines what redemption might look like, long after Richard is gone.
'Or that a generous brave man, as handsome as he used to be, as hopeful, and far more happy, may walk in the sunshine with him, honouring his grey head and saying to himself,'
'I thank God this is my father! Ruined by a fatal inheritance, and restored through me!'
She's imagining a grandson restoring a man she already knows is being destroyed.
And the phrase 'fatal inheritance' — it's doing double duty.
The money, yes — but also the legal trap, the name, the expectation that was always going to consume him.
And then there is the title itself — the house that carries this novel's name and its weight.
Esther, arriving at Jarndyce's home, reads the name written above the door.
'We went out of the porch and he showed me written over it, Bleak House.'
Seven words, and somehow they contain everything.
We'll pick up that thread — what the name carries, what home means in this novel — in our next segment.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Child and the City: Jo's Testimony Against Society

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the series in which we read Dickens's great novel closely, carefully, and with the attention it deserves.
I'm your host, and today we're examining one of the novel's most shattering sequences — the inquest into the death of the man known only as Nemo.
It's the moment when a street-sweeping boy named Jo is placed before a coroner and found, by the law, to be essentially no one.
With me today are three guests who bring very different lenses to this material.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose work on how Dickens builds his effects — sentence by sentence, image by image — is simply essential reading.

Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian, and the institutional machinery on display in these chapters — the inquest, the lawyers, the deliberate exclusions of the poor — is exactly his territory.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a critic who has lived with this novel since adolescence and reads it with a devotion that keeps catching new things.
Let's begin with Jo himself — what Dickens does in that extraordinary passage of testimony.
Every time I come back to Jo's testimony I find it almost unbearable to read — and I mean that as the highest praise Dickens can receive.
Dickens strips the boy down to almost nothing — not even a full name.
The passage reads like a legal deposition and an elegy at the same time.
Listen to how it opens — every phrase is a door slamming shut.
"Name, Jo. Nothing else that he knows on. Don't know that everybody has two names."
Three sentences, three negations — and already the whole social order has declared this child outside its reckoning.
And then that devastating list: "No father, no mother, no friends. Never been to school. What's home?"
What strikes me as a craft matter is how Dickens uses the third person to narrate what is essentially Jo speaking.
It's not quite free indirect discourse, not quite direct testimony — it's something stranger and more devastating.
The narrator becomes a kind of recording angel, translating the boy's inarticulate being into prose — but keeping the shape of his ignorance intact.
And notice the capital letters on HIM and HE — Dickens insisting, almost fiercely, that this boy has a selfhood.
The sentence is worth quoting in full — and I'll read it carefully.
"Don't know that Jo is short for a longer name. Thinks it long enough for HIM. HE don't find no fault with it."
That dignity — that quiet, obstinate dignity — is the whole moral argument of the passage in miniature.
Dickens is saying: this child cannot navigate your institutions, but he is not less than you.
It is worth being precise about what is actually happening in that courtroom — because the injustice is procedural before it is moral.
At mid-Victorian inquests, a witness could be excluded if they did not understand the nature of an oath — and a child who lacked religious instruction had no legal standing to swear one.
Jo's exclusion is not accidental cruelty — it is the system working exactly as designed.
Which makes the irony of Dickens's portrayal almost too sharp to look at directly.
The boy cannot swear an oath because no one taught him religion — yet Dickens shows us, in the very next breath, that Jo has a more instinctive moral sense than anyone in the room.
Here is the passage — and it is precise, not sentimental.
"Knows a broom's a broom, and knows it's wicked to tell a lie."
The law will not hear him — but he already knows what the law is supposed to protect.
And then there's the moment that breaks me every single time — when we learn how Jo and Nemo first met.
Dickens sets it up so plainly — a cold winter night, a boy shivering in a doorway, a man who turns to look at him.
And then Nemo — this man we know nothing about, this anonymous dead man — speaks four words that contain a whole philosophy of solidarity.
"Neither have I. Not one!"
He doesn't give Jo charity from a height — he places himself beside him.
And Dickens continues — the man would say in passing, "I am as poor as you to-day, Jo."
That repetition of Jo's name in that sentence — it's an act of recognition, almost of love.
Caroline has just put her finger on something architecturally important — Nemo and Jo mirror each other precisely.
Both are alone, both are nameless in their different ways — one literally, one through social erasure.
Dickens has structured their relationship as a kind of secret subplot running beneath the visible machinery of the plot.
And then the narrator turns to address Jo directly — which is one of the most formally audacious moves in the whole novel.
The omniscient narrator steps out of the narration entirely and speaks to the character — as if Dickens himself cannot maintain the fiction of distance.
He writes — and I find this extraordinarily moving as a technical choice —
"There is something like a distant ray of light in thy muttered reason for this: 'He wos wery good to me, he wos!'"
The dialect spelling of Jo's voice inside the narrator's elevated prose — that collision is the whole novel's moral logic in one sentence.
Before we leave the inquest entirely, I want to spend a moment with Mrs. Piper — because she is not merely comic relief.
Her testimony is a social document — it shows us how rumour functions as evidence in communities that have no other access to information.
Listen to how Dickens renders it — the syntax itself mimics the way gossip propagates, endlessly subordinated, never arriving.
"the plaintive—so Mrs. Piper insists on calling the deceased—was reported to have sold himself."
She cannot even name the legal term correctly — and yet her evidence about Nemo's relationship with Jo is buried in there, if you pick through the parentheses.
The court laughs her off — and in doing so, loses the only witness who saw Nemo and Jo together regularly.
Dickens is meticulous about showing us how incompetence and comedy combine to produce injustice.
That connection between comedy and institutional failure brings us directly to one of the novel's great satirical set pieces.
James, you've been looking at the Vholes passage from Chapter 39 — where Dickens turns the defence of legal practice into something approaching high farce.
The Vholes passage is, I think, the most formally sophisticated piece of legal satire in the whole novel — and the competition is fierce.

Dickens invents a parliamentary committee transcript — complete with numbered questions — and uses it to demonstrate how reform is defeated not by open corruption but by the invocation of respectability.
The attorney Mr. Kenge argues against changing the law on the grounds that it would destroy men like Vholes.
And the argument is delivered with such polished self-assurance that its absurdity almost escapes you the first time through.
Here is the pivot of the speech — and I'll read it at the pace it deserves.
"Sir, that class of practitioners would be swept from the face of the earth."
This is presented as a catastrophe — and Kenge continues, "the social system cannot afford to lose an order of men like Mr. Vholes."
The social system — not the clients, not the poor litigants ground to dust by delay — the social system.

And then the parliamentary committee concludes with a single devastating answer — "Mr. Vholes is considered, in the profession, a MOST respectable man" — which, Dickens tells us drily, proved fatal to the inquiry for ten years.
What I love about that passage is the mock-transcript form — Dickens is doing something almost experimental for 1852.
He is embedding a found document — a bureaucratic form — inside his novel's prose, and letting the form itself become the joke.
The question numbers are absurd — five hundred and seventeen thousand eight hundred and sixty-nine — and the absurdity is the point.
There have been so many questions, so many inquiries, so many numbered proceedings — and nothing has changed.
The bureaucracy satirizes itself simply by being accurately depicted.
And the link back to Jo is — I find it quietly devastating — that both passages end in the same structural place.
Jo is rejected by the inquest because the system cannot process him — and the Vholes committee shuts down reform because the system cannot threaten its own practitioners.
In both cases, the institution closes around itself like a fist.
And yet — and this is where Dickens refuses despair — there is that ray of light in Jo's case.
"He wos wery good to me, he wos" — that dialect, that grammar, that absolute simplicity — it is more eloquent than anything the court produced that day.
On that note — and I think it's exactly the right note to close on — Jo's simple grammar outlasting the court's elaborate machinery.
Thank you to Eleanor Hartley, James Blackstone, and Caroline Woodcourt for a conversation that has done real justice — perhaps more than the inquest managed — to this extraordinary material.
We'll be back with the next segment of Bleak House Unpacked very shortly.

segments.title: Laughter in the Darkness: Dickens's Comic Relief and Moral Purpose

utterances.text: Welcome to Bleak House Unpacked, the podcast that takes one of the great Victorian novels apart — slowly, lovingly, and with all the lights on.
I'm your host, and today we're asking a question that sounds simple but turns out to be quite rich: why is Bleak House so funny?
And more precisely — what is Dickens doing with that comedy, morally and structurally, in a novel so saturated with injustice and death?
To work through that, I have three exceptional readers with me today.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher whose great subject is how fiction is actually built — the architecture behind the effects we feel.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the institutions Dickens depicts — the courts, the class system, the machinery of Victorian life.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read Bleak House more times than she would perhaps admit — and who cares deeply about the experience of the reader on the page.
Caroline, let's begin with you, because you've always argued that the comedy starts on the very first page.
It does — and I think readers sometimes miss it on a first encounter because the atmosphere is so oppressive.
The fog, the mud, the dying sun — it feels genuinely apocalyptic.
And then Dickens drops in something so gloriously absurd that you almost do a double-take.
"It would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill."
A dinosaur, waddling through the legal district of London.
And the joke is that it wouldn't be out of place — that is the punchline.
The world is so primordially decayed, so pre-civilised in its filth, that a prehistoric monster would simply fit right in.
What I love about that sentence is the precision of the comedy — it's not a throwaway gag.
The Megalosaurus comes immediately after "foot passengers jostling one another's umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper."
Dickens has been cataloguing misery — dogs, horses, pedestrians — everything undignified and besmirched.
The dinosaur isn't an interruption to that register — it's the logical extreme of it.
The comedy and the horror are the same thing, pointed in the same direction.
There's also something very specific about the choice of Holborn Hill — that's not a random London street.
It's the route from the City, from the commercial and legal heart of London, toward the courts in Chancery Lane.
Dickens is placing his prehistoric monster on the precise path walked by lawyers and litigants every day.
The implication about the legal system is — shall we say — not flattering.
That makes the comedy even sharper — and it prepares the reader for Dickens's other great satirical target in the opening chapters, which is the fashionable world.
The portrait of Lady Dedlock's world in the second chapter is exquisitely funny — and exquisitely cruel.
She believes herself utterly inscrutable, utterly beyond the comprehension of the tradespeople around her.
And Dickens tells us, with perfect deadpan, that every single one of them knows her exact weaknesses.
The jewellers, the mercers, the librarian — they all have her completely mapped.
And then comes this remarkable image — I always stop at this.
"Who, in hooking one, hook all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet of the majestic Lilliput."
The great lady and her circle — reduced to a tiny fleet of toy ships, caught on a string.
The Gulliver comparison does something structurally brilliant — it reverses the expected power relation in a single image.
We think Lady Dedlock is a giant in her world — and she is, socially speaking.
But in Dickens's reframe she becomes the Lilliputian: tiny, easily managed, comically manipulated.
And what I find interesting is how that comedy lands alongside the genuine pathos Dickens will later build for her.
He makes her ridiculous first, so that her tragedy arrives with far more force.
What strikes me historically is how accurately Dickens had observed the relationship between the aristocracy and the luxury trades.
The notion that fashionable patronage could be manufactured — that Blaze and Sparkle or Sheen and Gloss could essentially engineer Lady Dedlock's tastes — that's not satire, exactly.
That's reportage.
The luxury trade in mid-Victorian London absolutely operated through this kind of studied flattery and deliberate influence over what the fashionable classes desired.
And Dickens, with that flat closing note — "in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not exaggerate at all" — is essentially confirming: this is real.
That deadpan confirmation is one of Dickens's great recurring moves — the straight face that condemns.
Caroline, you've said the comedy can also become something much stranger — almost gothic.
Yes — and the Snagsby passages are perhaps the clearest example of that in the whole novel.
Mr. Snagsby is a wonderfully mild figure — a law stationer, a man of no great will or agency.
And his wife's jealousy — her absolute certainty that he is concealing something from her — is played for comedy throughout.
But then Dickens writes this passage, and the comedy tips into something else entirely.
"Henceforth he begins, go where he will, to be attended by another shadow than his own, hardly less constant than his own, hardly less quiet than his own."
And then the clincher — "bone of his bone, flesh of his flesh, shadow of his shadow."
That's the marriage service — Genesis — biblical language turned into a curse.
It's funny, but it's also genuinely unsettling — and that double register is very distinctively Dickens.
The phrase "shadow of his shadow" is doing extraordinary work — it's where the comic grotesque fully shades into the sinister.
Because a shadow following a shadow is something that has no independent substance at all.
Mrs. Snagsby has become, in Dickens's framing, a kind of haunting — a spectral presence attached entirely to her husband's guilt, or what she imagines to be his guilt.
And notice that the chapter opened with a "ghostly shade, frilled and night-capped" — Dickens prepared that imagery before the passage even began.
The comedy of a suspicious wife becomes a meditation on surveillance, and on how a marriage can become a prison of mutual watching.
That surveillance theme is pervasive in the novel — it's not confined to domestic comedy.
Bucket watches Tulkinghorn; Tulkinghorn watches Lady Dedlock; Mrs. Snagsby watches Snagsby — the whole social architecture of the novel is built on hidden observation.
What's interesting is that when it's Mrs. Snagsby doing the watching, we're invited to laugh.
When it's the institutions — the lawyers, the detectives, the courts — the same behaviour becomes menacing.
The comedy is doing ideological work — it's calibrating our moral response to power based on who is wielding it.
That's a sharp and rather uncomfortable observation.
Let's end with one more passage — one that brings all of this together in a single scene of high comedy that is also, if you look closely, deeply revealing about Dickens's moral universe.
The scene with Smallweed and the will — late in the novel — is one of my absolute favourites for this quality.
Smallweed is a figure of undiluted avarice — almost a pantomime villain — and the business of the singed, stained will is played with considerable relish.
But then Bucket whispers — and it's in that whisper that the comedy hits its peak.
"There ain't one of the family that wouldn't sell the other for a pound or two, except the old lady — and she's only out of it because she's too weak in her mind to drive a bargain."
That last clause — the old lady is spared not by virtue but by incapacity — is Dickens at his darkest and most perfect.
There's no redemption available in this family — even the exception to the rule is not a moral exception.
And notice the delivery — Bucket whispers it, which means Esther is straining to catch the words.
The scene gives us the comedy of the Smallweed family, yes — but it's filtered through a detective who is simultaneously a performer.
Bucket's dexterity — Dickens actually uses the phrase "with the dexterity of a conjuror" — frames the whole transaction as a kind of theatrical trick.
And conjurors, of course, distract you with one hand while the real action happens elsewhere.
What this scene crystallises, legally and morally, is the sheer destructiveness of inheritance disputes.
The will has been singed, stashed, withheld — documents in Chancery could languish for decades while families destroyed themselves fighting over them.
And Bucket's sardonic accounting — twenty pounds laid out, grandchildren betraying grandfather on account of his living "so unreasonably long" — is not an exaggeration of the historical record.
The comedy is the documentary truth, served cold.
"Served cold" — that feels like the right temperature for Dickens's comedy throughout Bleak House.
What we've traced today is a comic mode that never operates separately from the moral vision — the laughter is the criticism.
The dinosaur, the jewellers, the watchful wife, the whispering detective — each is funny, and each is a small indictment.
My thanks to Eleanor, James, and Caroline for a conversation that was, I think, genuinely illuminating.
We'll be back with the next segment of Bleak House Unpacked shortly.

segments.title: The Web Tightens: Convergence and Consequences

utterances.text: We've reached the final movement of this episode, and it feels right to call it what it is: a reckoning.
The threads we've been tracing — secrets, power, identity, the slow grind of consequence — are beginning to converge.
Eleanor, James, Caroline — I want to start with Tulkinghorn, because he seems to me the hinge on which everything turns.
Tulkinghorn is one of the great architectural achievements of the novel, I think.
Dickens constructs him as a man who exists entirely in the negative space — defined by what he withholds.
There's this extraordinary passage when he first arrives at Chesney Wold at sunset.
"He carries family secrets in every limb of his body and every crease of his dress."
Every limb, every crease — the repetition is deliberate, almost incantatory.
Dickens is saying the secrets aren't just kept in Tulkinghorn's mind — they have colonised his very body.
And that physical quality isn't merely metaphor — it maps onto something real about the Victorian solicitor's role.
A family solicitor of Tulkinghorn's standing was genuinely a custodian of dynastic information — wills, debts, indiscretions, inheritances.
The law gave him access to the most intimate corners of a family's life.
What makes Dickens's portrait so unsettling is the line that follows Eleanor's quote.
"Whether his whole soul is devoted to the great or whether he yields them nothing beyond the services he sells is his personal secret."
We cannot tell whether he serves from loyalty or calculation.
That ambiguity is precisely what makes him dangerous — and precisely what real families feared in their solicitors.
What I keep returning to is the scene where he faces Lady Dedlock directly — and neither of them blinks.
Dickens renders it almost as a duel conducted entirely in stillness.
The passage builds to this extraordinary accumulation of questions.
"Whether each evermore watches and suspects the other, evermore mistrustful of some great reservation; whether each is evermore prepared at all points for the other, and never to be taken unawares."
Three times the word 'evermore' — and each time it tightens the screw a little further.
And then: what each would give to know how much the other knows.
That is the knife edge on which this whole story balances.
The structural brilliance there is that Sir Leicester is simply watching the fire throughout all of this.
He's physically present, he's the nominal head of the household — and he understands nothing.
Dickens gives us the Dedlock portrait on the staircase — that stately, frozen expression — as the image of Sir Leicester's inner life.
The man is a monument to a world that has already quietly crumbled beneath his feet.
And meanwhile, on the other side of this web, there is Esther — who doesn't yet know what she is to Lady Dedlock.
Jarndyce gives her the account of what little could be learned — and even that little is sealed off almost immediately.
The phrase that strikes me is the one about the woman's resolution — it's stated as an absolute.
"That more than this she would never — and he was well persuaded of the steadfastness of her resolution — for any human consideration disclose."
'Any human consideration' — that is a remarkable phrase to put into a legal account.
It tells you that Lady Dedlock has placed her secret outside the reach of normal moral leverage entirely.
And what happens when those secrets finally run out of room to hide?
There's a passage late in the novel — George Rouncewell walking through the empty rooms of Chesney Wold — that I find almost unbearable to read.
He's carrying a light, moving through the grandeur, and his mind is full of the murdered Tulkinghorn and the vanished Lady Dedlock.
Dickens writes it like this.
"He MIGHT see something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the darkness above and below."
That word 'blank' — twice, then again — is the sound of everything collapsing.
All that machinery of secrecy and suspicion — and at the end, just silence.
What I love about that passage is the word 'fancy' — the possibility that the horror might not be real, might be merely imagination.
But Dickens won't give George — or us — that comfort.
The blankness is worse than any spectre, because it means the catastrophe has already happened.
The secrets didn't stay secret — they detonated, and what's left is emptiness.
That image — grandeur hollowed out, light held up against blankness — feels like the novel's final word on what secrecy costs.
Eleanor, James, Caroline — this has been a remarkable conversation, and I'm grateful to all three of you.
Bleak House rewards exactly this kind of attention — the more closely you read it, the more it gives back.
If today's episode has sent you back to the novel — or sent you to it for the first time — that is everything we could hope for.
Thank you for listening to Bleak House Unpacked.

reasons for disdaining to utter something that you know; if so, pray,

passed in this family which she dearly loves, and relent, and help to
clear my son! My Lady, my good Lady,” the old housekeeper pleads with

woman than you were as boy and girl (your manhood will excuse me,
Rick!)—don’t be ashamed still to confide in me, for there will be

c13:p118.text:
“Come!” said Mr. Jarndyce. “Now for our assumption. Now we lift our
eyes up and look hopefully at the distance! Rick, the world is before
you; and it is most probable that as you enter it, so it will receive
you. Trust in nothing but in Providence and your own efforts. Never
separate the two, like the heathen waggoner. Constancy in love is a
good thing, but it means nothing, and is nothing, without constancy
in every kind of effort. If you had the abilities of all the great
men, past and present, you could do nothing well without sincerely
meaning it and setting about it. If you entertain the supposition
that any real success, in great things or in small, ever was or could
be, ever will or can be, wrested from Fortune by fits and starts,
leave that wrong idea here or leave your cousin Ada here.”

anything; and yet that’s my unhappy case. I was born into this
unfinished contention with all its chances and changes, and it began

since; and here I am now, conscious sometimes that I am but a
worthless fellow to love my confiding cousin Ada.”

as in the following blue minutes of a distinguished attorney’s
evidence. “Question (number five hundred and seventeen thousand eight
hundred and sixty-nine): If I understand you, these forms of practice

c1:p0.text:
London. Michaelmas term lately over, and the Lord Chancellor sitting
in Lincoln’s Inn Hall. Implacable November weather. As much mud in
the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of
the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus,
forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn
Hill. Smoke lowering down from chimney-pots, making a soft black
drizzle, with flakes of soot in it as big as full-grown
snowflakes—gone into mourning, one might imagine, for the death of
the sun. Dogs, undistinguishable in mire. Horses, scarcely better;
splashed to their very blinkers. Foot passengers, jostling one
another’s umbrellas in a general infection of ill temper, and losing
their foot-hold at street-corners, where tens of thousands of other
foot passengers have been slipping and sliding since the day broke
(if this day ever broke), adding new deposits to the crust upon crust
of mud, sticking at those points tenaciously to the pavement, and
accumulating at compound interest.
c1:p0.summary: London in November: fog and mud pervade the entire city, creating a primordial, apocalyptic atmosphere where even extinct creatures seem plausible.
c1:p0.best_quote: As much mud in the streets as if the waters had but newly retired from the face of the earth, and it would not be wonderful to meet a Megalosaurus, forty feet long or so, waddling like an elephantine lizard up Holborn Hill.

Has Mr. Tulkinghorn any idea of this himself? It may be so, or it may
not, but there is this remarkable circumstance to be noted in
everything associated with my Lady Dedlock as one of a class—as one
of the leaders and representatives of her little world. She supposes
herself to be an inscrutable Being, quite out of the reach and ken of
ordinary mortals—seeing herself in her glass, where indeed she looks
so. Yet every dim little star revolving about her, from her maid to
the manager of the Italian Opera, knows her weaknesses, prejudices,
follies, haughtinesses, and caprices and lives upon as accurate a
calculation and as nice a measure of her moral nature as her
dressmaker takes of her physical proportions. Is a new dress, a new
custom, a new singer, a new dancer, a new form of jewellery, a new
dwarf or giant, a new chapel, a new anything, to be set up? There are
deferential people in a dozen callings whom my Lady Dedlock suspects
of nothing but prostration before her, who can tell you how to manage
her as if she were a baby, who do nothing but nurse her all their
lives, who, humbly affecting to follow with profound subservience,
lead her and her whole troop after them; who, in hooking one, hook
all and bear them off as Lemuel Gulliver bore away the stately fleet
of the majestic Lilliput. “If you want to address our people, sir,”
say Blaze and Sparkle, the jewellers—meaning by our people Lady
Dedlock and the rest—“you must remember that you are not dealing
with the general public; you must hit our people in their weakest
place, and their weakest place is such a place.” “To make this
article go down, gentlemen,” say Sheen and Gloss, the mercers, to
their friends the manufacturers, “you must come to us, because we
know where to have the fashionable people, and we can make it
fashionable.” “If you want to get this print upon the tables of my
high connexion, sir,” says Mr. Sladdery, the librarian, “or if you
want to get this dwarf or giant into the houses of my high connexion,
sir, or if you want to secure to this entertainment the patronage of
my high connexion, sir, you must leave it, if you please, to me, for
I have been accustomed to study the leaders of my high connexion,
sir, and I may tell you without vanity that I can turn them round my
finger”—in which Mr. Sladdery, who is an honest man, does not
exaggerate at all.
c2:p12.summary: Despite believing herself inscrutable, Lady Dedlock is perfectly understood and managed by tradespeople and servants who deliberately lead her and her circle by flattery and careful study of her preferences.

The trooper, his old recollections awakened by the solitary grandeur
of a great house—no novelty to him once at Chesney Wold—goes up the
stairs and through the chief rooms, holding up his light at arm’s
length. Thinking of his varied fortunes within the last few weeks,
and of his rustic boyhood, and of the two periods of his life so
strangely brought together across the wide intermediate space;
thinking of the murdered man whose image is fresh in his mind;
thinking of the lady who has disappeared from these very rooms and
the tokens of whose recent presence are all here; thinking of the
master of the house upstairs and of the foreboding, “Who will tell
him!” he looks here and looks there, and reflects how he MIGHT see
something now, which it would tax his boldness to walk up to, lay his
hand upon, and prove to be a fancy. But it is all blank, blank as the
darkness above and below, while he goes up the great staircase again,
blank as the oppressive silence.
